slides.title: Should Parcelbird launch its own quick-commerce grocery delivery service in 2027?

paragraphs.text: Should Parcelbird launch its own quick-commerce grocery delivery service in 2027?
Assessment of the Parcelbird Now proposal and recommendation to the board · Board meeting, January 2027
Parcelbird
Board (two founders, two investors)
Prepared from the board briefing pack only (synthetic benchmark data); no external research

slides.title: Executive summary

paragraphs.text: Executive summary
Do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027; invest in the software business, which can reach profitability within current cash
The market is growing fast, but no operator makes money in it
–	Sales grew 42% a year in 2022–25, yet both incumbents lose money on every order
A Parcelbird store would lose money on every order, and customers don't stay long enough to repay their acquisition cost
–	A store loses $6.17 per order at the median; only the founders' plan, beyond any site observed, makes money
–	Our pop-up lost $12.57 per order, and only 22% of its customers still ordered in month 3
Even on the founders' own numbers, the launch breaks the investors' cash constraints
–	It needs $9.5M against $7.2M spendable above the runway floor; with core burn, cash runs out in month 13
The software business is a better use of the same cash
–	It breaks even in about month 26 at today's 60% growth and month 36 at 40%
–	It keeps 12 months of runway as long as ARR grows 34% a year or more
Decline the launch, back software-first in phased steps, and set triggers for any return to quick commerce
–	The launch case meets none of its six conditions; a 90-day checkpoint gates the second tranche of hires

Our Columbus pop-up trailed the benchmark median on all four drivers, leaving no evidence of a capability edge
Columbus pop-up (6 weeks, autumn 2026) against the benchmark median and the founders' plan
The one test of the founders' capability claim came in below the median
▪	The claim: "Our software already runs other people's dark stores, so we know how to run them better than anyone"
▪	Fair caveat, it was early: six weeks on a temporary site; orders grew 18% a week, from roughly 179 a day in week 1 to roughly 408 in week 6
▪	But growth was bought: it came with 12% promotions and $38 of acquisition cost per customer
▪	Ramp-up alone does not close the gap: even with every driver at the median, a store would still lose $6.17 per order
1  Pop-up site cost: $0.65M a year ÷ (280 × 365 orders) = $6.36 per order; rider cost: $17.75 ÷ 2.1 = $8.45 per order

3  Briefing pack figures are synthetic benchmark data

data: Contribution per order before site cost

paragraphs.text: Buying growth with promotions and paid social destroys value at these economics
▪	Median and pop-up: each order loses money before any site cost, so every customer acquired adds to the losses

slides.title: Zipcart's route to profit (a $3.99 fee, 1% promotions, 14% less volume) still leaves our median store losing $1.05 per order

paragraphs.text: 1 Market    2 Economics    3 Funding    4 Alternative    5 Decisions
Zipcart's route to profit (a $3.99 fee, 1% promotions, 14% less volume) still leaves our median store losing $1.05 per order
Median store contribution per order after site fixed cost, $, with Zipcart's Q4 2025 moves applied
A profitable route may exist, but only at top-quartile density with premium pricing
▪	What the investor update leaves out: Zipcart's +$0.40 per order was in its densest city only, after a new $3.99 fee on every order and promotions cut to 1%; volume there then fell 14%
▪	What it would take for us: with those moves, a median store earns +$3.02 before site cost and needs about 1,042 orders a day to cover $1.15M of site cost
▪	How far that is: 16% above today's median and 3.7 times the pop-up, with no loss of rider productivity at the lower volume
▪	Read-across: not where a new entrant starts, and nothing in our data shows it yet
1  Zipcart's moves from its shareholder letter as quoted in the briefing pack §11; volume loss applied to site cost only
2  Briefing pack figures are synthetic benchmark data

minimum annual ARR growth that keeps 12 months of runway
▪	60%, today's rate: break-even in month 26, low of $5.4M, runway never below about 24 months
▪	40%: break-even in month 36, low of $2.7M, runway at least 18 months
▪	34%: break-even in month 41, low of $1.2M, runway just holds at 12 months
▪	25% (not drawn): no break-even by month 48; cash runs out and the rule is breached

slides.title: We would reconsider an operator model only when customer sites prove the economics and dedicated funding exists

paragraphs.text: 1 Market    2 Economics    3 Funding    4 Alternative    5 Decisions
We would reconsider an operator model only when customer sites prove the economics and dedicated funding exists
Re-entry triggers for an operator model, reviewed quarterly from the data our software already collects across the 14 customer sites (no extra cost)
1. Site-level profit is proven
2. The profit drivers are seen at one site at the same time
3. Customers stay
4. Funding is ring-fenced
▪	At least one customer site shows positive contribution after site cost for two consecutive quarters
▪	Today: none
▪	Best-observed inputs give −$1.76 per order
▪	AOV of $42 or more and 3.0 or more orders per rider-hour at 1,050 or more orders a day, or a service fee that does the same job without losing more than 15% of volume
▪	Today: no site has both
▪	Break-even with Zipcart's moves needs about 1,042 orders a day
▪	Month-3 retention high enough to repay $38 of acquisition cost within 12 months at actual contribution
▪	Today: 22% at 3.1 orders a month
▪	Payback never happens at the median
▪	Dedicated capital that leaves the core business with 12 months of runway at all times
▪	Today: a new round is "unlikely"
▪	Headroom is $7.2M against a $9.5M plan
1  Thresholds set by the analysis: 1,050 orders a day rounds up the 1,042 break-even (p. 14); the 15% volume limit sits just above Zipcart's 14% loss
